title: Symphony No. 5 in E minor
hook: One gloomy tune walks through all four movements and comes out the other side as a march.

painting.title: Morning in a Pine Forest
painting.pairingNote: Painted the year after the symphony, a dark Russian forest slowly filling with morning light; the same road from gloom to brightness that the motto theme travels.

facts: Tchaikovsky wrote the Fifth between May and August 1888, mostly at Frolovskoye, the country house where he was then living. It came ten years after the Fourth, and while writing it he kept doubting that he could still compose.

In a notebook that spring he sketched a programme: “Total submission before fate, or, what is the same thing, the inscrutable designs of Providence”. Yet in June he told a correspondent that the symphony had no programme. How much of the plan survived is not known.

A single theme, often called the motto, is heard in all four movements: funereal at the start, a troubling ghost in the middle movements, a blazing march at the end. The keys travel the same way, from E minor to E major.

Tchaikovsky conducted the first performance in St Petersburg on 17 November 1888. After the first few performances he decided it was a failure, “too colourful, massive, insincere”. A few months later, after a concert in Hamburg, he loved it again. It is dedicated to Theodor Avé-Lallemant, head of the Hamburg Philharmonic Society.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dark march and a restless dance (I), a love song on the horn (II), a graceful waltz with a shadow (III), the motto’s triumph (IV).

movements.heading: Andante – Allegro con anima
movements.summary: Two clarinets, low and dark, play the motto as a slow funeral march. Then a quick, restless dance begins, and the movement becomes a struggle between that nervous energy and a broad, warm second theme. It ends as it began, in the dark: quiet, low and in E minor.

mainIdeas.name: The motto
mainIdeas.description: a slow, heavy tune in the low clarinets, like a funeral march.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, slightly limping dance in 6/8, first on clarinet and bassoon.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a broad, yearning melody in the strings, in D major.

stops.hear: Two clarinets, low and dark, play a slow, solemn tune over hushed strings
A quiet, nervous pulse in the strings; clarinet and bassoon start a lilting, dance-like tune
The strings press on with a more urgent idea; the full orchestra joins
stops.happening: A second idea in the first group, then the climb to a climax

stops.hear: A short sighing figure passes between strings and woodwinds
The violins sing a broad, warm, longing melody, a little slower
stops.happening: Theme 2, in D major (*Molto più tranquillo*)

stops.hear: The dance tune is broken up and tossed around, building to loud, clashing climaxes
The dance tune returns quietly in the low woodwinds
The broad melody again, rising to a last big climax

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: The dance tune is hammered out, then sinks; the movement ends very softly in the depths of the orchestra

notice: Remember the clarinets’ tune from the first minute. It will come back in every movement.
Listen to the last bars: the music does not end with a bang but goes down into the bassoons and low strings and fades.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Recorded at a concert in the Philharmonie, Berlin, on 9 March 2019, a few months before Kirill Petrenko became the Berliner Philharmoniker’s chief conductor in August 2019. The recording came out in 2020, on its own and in a box set of his first recordings with the orchestra.

movements.heading: Andante cantabile, con alcuna licenza
movements.summary: One of the most famous horn solos ever written. After a few dark chords in the low strings, the horn sings a long, tender melody; an oboe joins it. A more agitated middle section, led by the clarinet, builds to an outburst in which the motto crashes in. The love song returns, grander, and the motto interrupts it a second time.

mainIdeas.name: The horn melody
mainIdeas.description: slow, soft and very long, marked *dolce con molto espressione*.

mainIdeas.name: The second tune
mainIdeas.description: a shorter, rising phrase for oboe and horn.

stops.hear: Slow, dark chords in the low strings, moving from minor towards major
stops.happening: The introduction, from B minor to D major

stops.hear: A solo horn sings a long, tender melody over soft strings
stops.happening: The horn solo, the main theme

stops.hear: An oboe answers with a shorter, rising phrase; horn and oboe share it
The cellos and then the violins take the horn’s melody, warm and full
Faster and more uneasy: a clarinet starts a restless, searching tune
The brass blast out the motto from the first movement
The horn’s melody returns in the violins, now broader
The whole orchestra swells to the movement’s biggest climax
stops.happening: The love song at full strength

stops.hear: The motto again, at full force

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: Quiet: the melody is remembered in pieces, and the movement fades on a soft chord

notice: Listen for how freely the horn shapes its melody. *Con alcuna licenza* means “with some freedom”: the tempo bends with the phrase.
The motto now sounds like a threat from outside. Each time, the love song has to recover.

movements.heading: Valse: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A waltz takes the place of the usual scherzo. The tune is graceful but slightly lopsided, with phrases that do not quite fit the beat. The middle is a flurry of fast, whispering notes in the strings. Near the end the motto drifts through, softly, in waltz time, like a shadow crossing a ballroom.

mainIdeas.name: The waltz
mainIdeas.description: a lilting tune in the violins, with little hesitations.

mainIdeas.name: The flurry
mainIdeas.description: fast, light running notes passed through the strings.
The motto, quietly, in the woodwinds.

stops.hear: The violins play a graceful waltz tune over a light accompaniment
An oboe and then the bassoon add new, gently lilting tunes
The strings break into fast, whispering running notes, passed from section to section
The waltz returns, and the running notes continue around it
stops.happening: The waltz with the trio’s texture

stops.hear: Clarinets and bassoons, very softly, play the motto in three-time
stops.happening: The motto, now as a waltz

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Six loud chords from the whole orchestra

notice: Try to count the waltz in threes. Here and there the rhythm seems to shift into twos, a [[hemiola|hemiola]].
Listen for the motto near the end. It is so quiet it is easy to miss.

movements.heading: Finale: Andante maestoso – Allegro vivace
movements.key: E major – E minor – E major
movements.summary: The motto returns at the start, now in E major and played by the strings like a hymn. Then a fierce Allegro breaks out. The finale is a hard-driven race, and at its end the motto becomes a grand march in the brass. In the last pages, the trumpets play the first movement’s dance tune, now in triumph.

mainIdeas.name: The motto in the major
mainIdeas.description: broad and solemn at first, triumphant at the end.

mainIdeas.name: The Allegro’s main theme
mainIdeas.description: a fierce, stamping tune in the strings.
A second, more lyrical theme in the woodwinds.

stops.hear: The strings play the motto, slowly and solemnly, now in a warm major key
stops.happening: The introduction, *Andante maestoso*, in E major

stops.hear: Suddenly fast: a fierce, driving tune in the strings
A smoother, more lyrical tune in the woodwinds, over the running strings
The brass blaze out the motto in the middle of the race
The fierce tune again, with a new melody laid over it
A huge cadence and a pause; it sounds like the end, but it is not
The motto as a grand, slow march for the whole orchestra, led by the brass
stops.happening: The coda, *Moderato assai e molto maestoso*, in E major

stops.hear: Suddenly very fast, with the strings in a whirl

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Trumpets and horns play the first movement’s dance tune, broad and loud, in E major; final chords

notice: Compare the first two minutes with the very first minute of the symphony: the same tune, now in the major and in the strings instead of the clarinets.
After the big pause near the end, notice how slow the march is. Tchaikovsky himself thought this ending overdone; listen and decide.

threads.title: The motto
threads.body: One tune through four movements: a funeral march (I), an intruder (II), a shadow in waltz time (III), a hymn and a victory march (IV). This is [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]].

threads.title: Minor to major
threads.body: The symphony moves from E minor to E major, the path Beethoven’s Fifth made famous.

threads.title: Doubt
threads.body: Tchaikovsky wrote it doubting himself, judged it harshly, then changed his mind. He was never sure the triumphant ending rang true.

threads.title: Melody first
threads.body: The horn solo, the waltz and the second themes show his gift for long, singing lines, often given to a single wind instrument.
